sections.text: पुरुषः स परः पार्थ भक्त्या लभ्यस्त्वनन्यया।
*Now I will tell thee, O Arjuna, of the times at which, if the mystics go forth, they do not return, and at which they go forth only to return.

If knowing the Supreme Spirit the sage goes forth with fire and light, in the daytime, in the fortnight of the waxing moon and in the six months before the Northern summer solstice, he will attain the Supreme.
Fire, light, daytime, the bright fortnight, the six months of the northern solstice , departing by this path, the knowers of God go to God.

We had been discussing chapter eight, Imperishable Brahman. We are coming to the last concluding verses of this chapter. In chapter seven, we learned about the nature of the supreme as the Higher Prakriti and the Lower Prakriti.
He said, my Lower Prakriti is Eightfold Prakriti which is manifest. My Higher Prakriti which supports this lower Prakriti. So that higher Prakriti is the imperishable Brahman, which is the substratum for this Lower Prakriti.
That which is manifest is supported by that which is Unmanifest. That Unmanifest is the Supreme Brahman, the Imperishable. So chapter eight is our quest to understand the imperishable Brahman.
Weve been discussing the nature of the Imperishable Brahman. In the beginning we have learned that the nature of that supreme reality is imperishable. He is self knowing and in his work is to create these things and beings.
That same supreme reality creates these things and beings as Prakriti -- the Lower Prakriti, out of his own self. So the world which we see is the manifest world, but it is supported by the Unmanifest. The Unmanifest is imperishable, but the world which it creates is perishable.
Prakriti is infinite, just as Brahman is infinite. Prakriti is ever-existing, just as Brahman is ever-existing. But the creations within Prakriti are perishable, because the same entity which creates these things and beings will keep creating and destroying.
Brahma, the Creator, while he is working -- thats his day. When hes not working, thats his night. And we have seen that how long the Brahmas day is compared to hours.
Then in the end we have talked about how can the individual ego, the individual entity which finds itself to be limited by these limitations of mind and intellectual, can rise above this limitations and reach the Supreme. Why Im suffering through my limitations. And therefore there are Sorrows.
If I was having no limitation, there will not be any sorrow. So my quest in life is to get over all my limitations. So when I transit from one existence to another, my goal is always to get to a stage which has less limitations or no limitations.
So we talked about the one who dies with that thought of imperishable in mind will lead the imperishable. One who dies with the goal of achieving something will get to that state of achievement. Those who worship Devas will go to Devas.
Those who worship Brahman will go to Brahman. Then we elaborately discussed how to get to that point where we can think about that goal. Verse 21, which was the last one we discussed, says: Avyakto Akshara iti uktah tam ahuh paramam gatim.
That which is considered the unmanifest, imperishable -- that is your highest goal. They who reach it never again return. Yam prapya na nivartante.
Everyone else has to come back because of some goal or other. Some desire or other which is unfulfilled. And I want to fulfill it.
I want to achieve their capabilities and then achieve that goal. So to achieve that, now Im in a pursuit of happiness. Because my happiness is somewhere else.
I have to come back to pursue my happiness. But one who wants to achieve that happiness which is supreme, then he doesnt have to come back. And therefore it says that your goal is to achieve that unmanifest and imperishable that is considered the highest goal.
They who reach it never again return. Bhagwan says, that is my highest abode. Thats what my my abode is.
All this time we had been discussing and thinking about what is the nature of the Lord and where does he reside. He says, that is my abode and thats my nature. My nature is supreme, imperishable, unmanifest.
My abode is that state of awareness -- thats where you will find me. So the next seven verses, which are the concluding verses, say: Purushah sa parah partha bhaktya labhyas tu ananyaya. Is it ever possible to achieve that state of oneness with the imperishable Brahman? Right now I can achieve oneness with my own limitations -- this is me. I can also relate to other things in the world and achieve oneness.
But it is unthinkable right now to achieve oneness with the supreme imperishable Brahman. Bhagavan gives a guarantee here: it is achievable by Bhaktya labhyas tu ananyaya -- by single-pointed devotion. Single-pointed identification with that imperishable Brahman.
As long as Im identified with something else, I cannot be identifying with that. As long as Im identified with my body, my intellect there is no way that I can identify with him. So Bhagavan said, it is possible for Purusha, any person to achieve that by single pointed devotion.
Thats the only path. Yasyantahasthani Bhutani. That single pointed devotion for what? That which is the indwelling for all beings.
I am trying to achieve understanding about myself. But in that inward journey I have to realize that myself is not just limited to my limited self but it is the self of all the beings. Yesyanta sthani Bhutani.
Thats the dwelling place for all beings. Yena sarvam idam tatam -- everything is pervaded by it. That entity with which I want to identify is the dwelling place for all beings and things.
With single-pointed devotion, Im identifying with that. We can very easily identify with people and things similar to us. We have difficulty identifying with people who are a little different from us.
They speak different language, they look different. Its a way I can overcome that. But then I have to identify with entire Jagat and it goes even beyond that and says there is nothing in this universe cosmos where the self is not pervaded.
In my inward journey of meditation I have to understand and identify with that entity which does not leave anything out. If I say I love this, but I hate this, well, I have limited him. I created limitation for him and therefore my journey is incomplete.
So now Bhagavan said that I will explain to you how to reach there. And he said there are two paths. Yatra kale to anavrutyam avruttim chevayogina.
Well, first qualification. You should be a Yogi. You are the one who is striving to achieve this liberation thats given.
But the striving alone will not guarantee that you will achieve liberation. Because the path you may take. He said he will explain the time and path while parting from this state of existence: one which is the path of return, and one which is the path of no return.
We have been trying -- people have been trying -- but we continue to come back to the same world of sorrow. Prayatha Yanti Tamkalam Vakyami Bharata Sabah. So I will let you know what path will lead you to no return.
I also let you know what the path of return. So thats basically just an introduction to the next two verses. Next is Agnihi Jyotihi Ahaha, Shuklaha Shanmasa, Uttarayanam Tatra, Prayahata, Gachanti, Brahma, Brahma Vidojanaha.
These two mantas are very, very difficult to understand because from a superficial translation it makes no sense whatsoever. It says Agni, Jyoti, Ahaha -- fire, light, daytime -- Shuklaha, the bright fortnight, in six months of Uttarayanam. Tatra Prayata Gachanti Brahma, Brahma Vidojanaha -- one who goes through that path, they go to Brahman, the path of no return.
The Yogi who knows Brahman goes through this path of light. So now, if we take this literally, that means people who die during these six months have a chance to get liberated, and the other six months have no chance. December 22 to June 21 you get liberation, and after June 22 to December 21 people have to return.
That obviously makes no sense. You have to remember the Gita is the essence of Upanishads. Sarva Upanishado Gavo, Dugdham Gopala Nandanam -- all Upanishads are cows, and Gopala Nandana (Krishna) has collected the milk and given it to you.
He is the one who collected all the ideas and concepts from the Upanishads and put them in the Bhagavad Gita. You have to study the Upanishads to understand these concepts. These particular two verses about the path of Uttarayana and Dakshinayana are directly taken from the Prashna Upanishad.
The Prashna Upanishad elaborately explains the path of Uttarayana and Dakshinayana. It starts with explaining the creation of this universe -- that Prajapati himself became the sun and the moon. The sun represents energy; the moon represents matter.
Then it also explains how the year is created, how a month is created, how a day is created -- one represents energy, the other matter. Anything during the day represents energy. We know that daytime is the domain of the sun -- sunlight, energy, activity.
Nighttime is presided over by the moon -- its inactivity. Darkness -- thats the path of the Moon. So the two paths were thought of as the path of energy and the path of matter; the path of the Sun.
With Krama Mukti, the gradual liberation through Upasana and Karmas, you reach through the path of the sun to the Brahmaloka. We also know that we can gradually improve ourselves. So the good actions are necessary.
But we also know that doing good is not good enough. It has to be associated with knowledge. So that is the difference between the two parts.
One who is doing good but with a goal of getting something good out of it -- that is the path of return. One who is doing good but without seeking anything in return, seeking only to liberate himself -- those selfless actions are the path of no return. These two are symbolically described in Upanishadic language as the Path of Uttarayana and the Path of Dakshinayana.
Another way to look at it: when we face the sun in the morning, we are facing east. On your right side is south, and your left side is north. So the path of Dakshinayana is the sun rising from the east, going through the south, and setting in the west.
The path of the north is the path of the rising sun. And the path of the south is the path of the setting sun. So we are going from the rising sun to daytime, from the setting sun to nighttime.
If we associate knowledge and the sacred with the path of the rising sun, that is the path of Uttarayana; the path of the setting sun is the path of Dakshinayana. Both describe the mental makeup of a yogi -- one who is seeking liberation versus one who will come back to enjoy. If you listen to political conventions, if you just look at how the nominee is described, it looks like theyre sages.
Theyre only driven by the common good. They just wanted to do nothing but help people. So if that is true, then hes a sage.
But if you take that and see that they are not only doing good, but they also have their own good in mind. They want to achieve something out of it. At the path of return, youre constantly coming back to do good so that you can get something out of it.
Bhagawan said it is exactly the same for the yogi. The Prashna Upanishad describes in detail that those who want to gain something out of their good actions are on the path of return. And we have seen in earlier verses that during Brahmas night, all beings are in a dormant state, and when creation starts, they emerge from whatever unfulfilled desires remain and come back into this universe again.

Bhaktya labhyas tu ananyaya, the Supreme is attainable through single-pointed devotion alone. This verse addresses a common concern: Is liberation actually possible for ordinary people like us? Krishna answers emphatically: yes, but the key is ananya, undivided, exclusive devotion. This does not mean abandoning responsibilities; it means having only one ultimate allegiance while performing all duties. Examine your divided loyalties today. We easily identify with people similar to us but struggle with those who appear different. Yet the teaching says we must identify with that in which all beings abide and which pervades the entire universe. This week, practice expanding your circle of identification. When you meet someone who seems very different from you, look for the common awareness that animates both of you. That shared consciousness is the Supreme Self dwelling equally in all.
Verses 23-24 introduce the symbolic paths of Uttarayana (northern course) and Dakshinayana (southern course). Rather than being literal astronomical timings for death, these represent mental and spiritual states. The path of fire, light, daytime, bright fortnight symbolizes the illuminated mind filled with knowledge. The opposite path represents the mind clouded with ignorance and attachment. The practical question becomes: What path is your mind currently traveling? Is it moving toward greater light, clarity, and selflessness (Uttarayana)? Or toward greater attachment, confusion, and self-centeredness (Dakshinayana)? The good news is that unlike the literal suns path, your mental path can be changed at any moment through conscious choice. Today, notice moments when your mind moves toward darkness, worry, resentment, craving, and gently redirect it toward light. Each redirection is a practice run for the ultimate journey.
